pif_form.instruction_text:
In order for the Artificial Intelligence to create the best plan for your child, we need a true picture of their reality. Follow these 7 golden rules:

1. Observe daily life: Evaluate the child in their natural routine, without forcing tests.
2. One action at a time: Each option evaluates an isolated skill. Focus only on what is written.
3. The '3 out of 5' Rule: Only check the option if the child can perform the action ALONE (without verbal prompts or physical help) in at least 3 out of every 5 attempts.
4. Once done, always done: Mark the skills the child does today or has successfully done in the past, such as babbling, rolling, crawling, etc., even if they have stopped doing them.
5. Be 100% honest: Omitting or masking difficulties directly harms the result of the Intervention Plan. Answer based on reality, not expectations.
6. When in doubt, leave it blank: If the child only does it with a lot of help or you are not absolutely sure, leave it unchecked. It is better to focus on what is already guaranteed.
7. If this is not the child's first PIF, observe if the child has lost any essential skills (talking, walking, playing with other children, etc.). If this occurs, uncheck the option on the form.

⚠️ IMPORTANT WARNING: Cognacare structures the Intervention Plan based exclusively on your answers. If the information provided is inaccurate, incomplete, or unrealistic, the generated plan will be ineffective. The responsibility for the accuracy of the data lies entirely with the person filling out the form.

play_questions.exploratory_1: The child often puts fingers or hands in their mouth (e.g., sucks thumb, hand, or any small object they grab)

play_questions.functional_1: The child rolls a ball down a ramp or pushes a toy car (uses the toy for its intended purpose)

play_questions.functional_3: The child stacks blocks in different ways (e.g., makes a tower by stacking one on top of the other, places side by side in sequence, creates a bridge)
play_questions.functional_4: The child kicks a ball aiming to hit something (e.g., tries to make the ball go towards a target or in a certain direction)

play_questions.functional_6: The child places small pieces exactly where they fit (e.g., puts coins in a piggy bank, fits pieces into specific holes)
play_questions.functional_7: The child imitates simple actions they see an adult do with toys (e.g., sees adult banging with a hammer and tries to do the same)
play_questions.functional_8: The child purposely repeats the same action several times with a toy (e.g., fits and removes a piece repeatedly, opens and closes a box several times)

play_questions.symbolic_1: The child pretended an object is something completely different (e.g., a pencil becomes a magic wand, a stick becomes a spoon, sits on a chair and says they are driving a car)
play_questions.symbolic_2: The child uses invisible (imaginary) things in play as if they were real (e.g., makes motions of washing hair with non-existent shampoo, or pretends to turn a key to start an invisible car)
play_questions.symbolic_3: The child creates a sequence of actions that make sense and connect logically (e.g., first puts the doll in bed, then covers with blanket, then turns off light)

play_questions.games_rules_1: The child understands they have to wait their turn and waits when it is someone else's turn to play (e.g., in a game, watches while other plays and then plays when it is their turn)
play_questions.games_rules_2: The child gives up what they want to do so as not to spoil the game and maintain friendship (e.g., wants to take a piece, but sees they can't because it's not the game rule)

privacy_policy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy_policy.intro: Welcome to the Cognacare Family Intervention Plan (PIF) platform ({{siteUrl}}). Your privacy is important to us. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, share, and protect your personal information and the information of the children registered on the platform, in compliance with the General Data Protection Law (LGPD - Law No. 13.709/2018), GDPR, and other applicable regulations.
privacy_policy.section1_text: {{razaoSocial}}, registered under CNPJ No. {{cnpj}} ("Cognacare"), is the data controller of the personal data processed through the platform. This Policy applies to the users who are the legal guardians of the children, invited professionals, affiliates, and other visitors who use our digital services.
privacy_policy.section2_intro: We collect different types of information to provide and improve our services:

section2_list.user_info: User Registration Information: Name, email address, CPF (when necessary for tax purposes), optional phone number, and password (stored encrypted) when you create an account.
section2_list.child_info: Child Information: Data voluntarily provided by you, such as name, date of birth, diagnoses, and developmental characteristics, essential for customizing our educational support and family routine services, which do not constitute medical diagnosis. The processing of this data is always carried out in the best interest of the child and with the specific consent of the legal guardian.
section2_list.pif_data: PIF Form Data: Detailed responses regarding the child's development and family context, used to generate customized documents.
section2_list.chat_history: Chat History: Content of interactions with the AI Assistant, used to improve the experience and contextualize the support.
section2_list.financial: Financial Information: Transaction history, subscribed plans, credits, and balances. Complete credit card data is processed exclusively by a secure payment gateway (Efi Pay) and is not stored by Cognacare.
section2_list.usage: Usage Information: Technical data such as IP address, device identifiers, access logs, cookies, and browsing data, collected for security, fraud prevention, and experience improvement purposes.
section2_list.affiliate: Affiliate Data: Name, email, CPF or CNPJ (when applicable), PIX key, bank details necessary for payment, history of sales attributed to your link or coupon, performance metrics, and public social media profile information used in the evaluation process.

section3_list.legal_obligation: Compliance with Legal Obligations: Issuance of tax documents, maintenance of records for accounting purposes, and compliance with legal retention periods.
section3_list.legitimate_interest: Legitimate Interest: To monitor platform use, prevent fraud, improve features, conduct statistical analysis, and manage the Affiliate Program, always respecting your fundamental rights and freedoms.
section3_list.consent_child: Consent: Processing of children's personal data, with the specific and prominent consent of the legal guardian, always in the best interest of the minor.
section3_list.communication: Communications: To send generated documents, important account notices, plan updates, and contractual changes. Promotional messages will only be sent when permitted by applicable law, with an opt-out option.

privacy_policy.section5_text: Registration and use of the platform must be carried out by the child's legal guardian or by a professional duly authorized by that guardian. We always act based on the principle of the best interest of the child.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Cognacare, FIPs, and our Artificial Intelligence.

items.question: What is Cognacare?
items.answer: Cognacare is an AI-powered platform designed to support atypical families and healthcare professionals. Our tool helps structure routines, adapt play, and create personalized Family Intervention Plans (FIP) tailored to each child's sensory profile and diagnosis.

items.question: Does Cognacare replace medical therapy or professional guidance?
items.answer: No. Cognacare is a parental and educational SUPPORT tool. The suggestions generated by our Artificial Intelligence do not replace diagnoses, medical treatments, or the monitoring by trained professionals (neurologists, occupational therapists, speech therapists, psychologists, etc.). Always validate the suggested activities with the child's therapy team.

items.question: What is a FIP?
items.answer: FIP stands for Family Intervention Plan. It is a document generated by our AI that translates developmental needs into practical, playful activities to be done at home. It takes into account the child's hyperfocus, triggers, dietary restrictions, and sensory profile to ensure that the activities are welcoming and functional.

items.question: How does the Credit and Chat system work?
items.answer: Cognacare operates on a balance system. You use 'FIP Credits' to generate new comprehensive plans, and 'Chat Credits' to converse with the AI Assistant (each sent and received message consumes credits). You can purchase extra packages or subscribe to one of our Premium Plans for automatic recharges and exclusive benefits.

items.question: Can I register more than one child on the same account?
items.answer: Yes! You can create separate profiles for different children under your account. Our AI will treat each profile independently, ensuring that the FIP and Chat interactions are 100% focused on the specific characteristics of that individual child.

items.question: How does the Affiliate program work?
items.answer: Selected users can become Cognacare Affiliates. By sharing your exclusive link or coupon, you offer discounts to new families and earn a commission for every subscription or credit package sold. You can track your sales and earnings directly from your dashboard.

items.question: Are my data and my child's data secure?
items.answer: The security and privacy of your family are our top priority. The data entered (such as age, diagnosis, and sensory profile) is used exclusively by the AI engine to personalize your experience during generation. We do not sell or share sensitive data with third parties.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Translate 'therapy-speak' into plain English. Understand technical terms and acronyms of atypical child development.
glossary.search_placeholder: Search for a term, acronym, or therapy...

terms.definition: A science that studies human behavior. In child therapies, it is used to teach useful skills (like speaking, playing, and interacting) and reduce harmful behaviors, always focusing on how the environment influences the child.
In ABA vocabulary, a 'mand' is simply the act of REQUESTING something the child wants or needs (e.g., saying 'water' when thirsty, or pointing to a toy).
In ABA vocabulary, a 'tact' is the act of NAMING or commenting on something the child sees, hears, or feels (e.g., seeing a dog on the street and saying 'dog!', without wanting to pet the dog).
The ability to exactly repeat what the other person just said, like an echo.
A good consequence (a reward, praise, a smile, a toy) that happens right after the child does something expected, which increases the chances of them repeating that good behavior in the future.
A therapeutic strategy that consists of withholding attention or reward for an inappropriate behavior, with the goal of making that behavior stop.

The process of building a bond of trust with the child. The adult associates themselves with the things the child likes most, showing that their presence is fun and safe, before starting to demand any tasks.
The ability of the child (or adult) to recognize, manage, and respond to a strong emotion (like anger, frustration, or excessive joy) in an appropriate and healthy way.

An intense crisis caused by sensory or emotional overload. It is not a 'tantrum' to get something, but rather a total loss of brain control due to an excess of stimuli. The child cannot stop even if they want to.

The opposite of a Meltdown. Faced with sensory or emotional overload, the child's brain 'turns off'. They retreat, stop talking, do not react to stimuli, and isolate themselves physically and mentally.

A set of brain skills that acts like the 'conductor of an orchestra'. It involves the ability to plan tasks, maintain focus, remember instructions, control impulses, and transition from one activity to another.

The repetition of sounds, words, or phrases that the child heard (from people, cartoons, or songs). It can occur immediately after hearing or days later. It is often used by the child to self-soothe or attempt to communicate.
Repetitive body movements or sounds (like hand-flapping, toe-walking, rocking, or making vocal sounds). They are primarily used for emotional or sensory self-regulation.
The way the brain receives, organizes, and interprets information that comes from the senses (sight, hearing, touch, smell, taste, plus balance and body awareness).
Basic self-care tasks necessary for independence in everyday life, such as bathing, dressing, using the toilet, brushing teeth, and eating independently.
The use of tools (like picture boards, tablets with speech apps, or sign language) to help people who are non-speaking or have speech difficulties to express themselves and be understood.
An extremely intense and prolonged interest in a specific subject, object, or activity (e.g., dinosaurs, fans, letters). The child focuses a large part of their attention on it.
The child has perfect hearing in their ears, but the brain has difficulty interpreting and understanding what was heard, especially in noisy environments.

A neurological motor speech disorder. The child knows what they want to say, but the brain has difficulty planning and coordinating the exact movements of the lips, tongue, and jaw needed to produce the word's sound.
A behavioral disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of irritability, stubbornness, frequent arguments, and defiance toward authority figures (parents, teachers).

A neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication, interactions, and the presence of restricted and repetitive behaviors, interests, or activities. It is called a 'spectrum' because it affects each person in a unique way.

Current clinical classification for ASD (Level 1, 2, or 3). Replaces older terms like 'Asperger's' or 'Mild/Severe Autism'. Indicates the amount of help and adaptation the person needs for daily activities.

A neurobiological disorder that includes inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. The child may have difficulty focusing on tasks outside their extreme interests or act without thinking about consequences.

The brain's difficulty in receiving and responding to information coming through the senses. The child may be hypersensitive (feels pain from common noises or textures) or hyposensitive (constantly seeks impact, jumping, or deep pressure).

A temporary diagnosis given to children under 5 who do not meet expected developmental milestones in several areas (speech, motor, social), but are still too young for a definitive diagnosis like ASD or Intellectual Disability.
A specific learning disorder that affects the ability to read and recognize words fluently, regardless of the child's intelligence.
Also known as Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD). It affects motor planning and coordination, making the child appear 'clumsy' when running, writing, using utensils, or tying shoes.
Considered the 'gold standard' assessments for an Autism diagnosis. ADOS-2 is an observation play session with the child, and ADI-R is an in-depth interview with the parents.

One of the most famous assessments in ABA therapy. It measures language development milestones and identifies 'barriers' (what is stopping the child from learning, such as disruptive behaviors or visual perception flaws).

A detailed mapping of the brain conducted by a specialized psychologist. Through tests and games, it measures intelligence (IQ), memory, attention, reasoning, and executive functions to help reach a diagnosis.

A legally mandated school document for inclusive education. It is a roadmap created by the school (often alongside therapists) that adapts the curriculum, tests, and teaching methods to the reality of that specific child.
A therapy focused on very young children (ages 1 to 4) with autism. It combines the principles of ABA science with natural play, applied in a highly playful and relationship-focused manner.
A specific alternative communication protocol. The child is taught to pick up a picture of what they want and hand it to an adult to get the item, encouraging communication initiation.

A therapeutic approach that repeats the natural phases of a baby's neuro-psychomotor development (such as rolling, creeping, and crawling) to try to reorganize the nervous system and improve speech, chewing, and movement.

A therapy widely used in physical and speech therapy for neurological rehabilitation. It focuses on inhibiting abnormal movement patterns and facilitating correct postures, very common in Cerebral Palsy cases.

An educational program that focuses on the visual organization of the environment. It uses boards, colors, and physical space separation to help people with autism understand routines and gain independence at work or school.
A person whose neurological and cognitive development follows the expected and majority pattern of the population. It is the opposite of neurodivergent.
A term encompassing people whose brains function, learn, and process information differently than the typical pattern (includes people with Autism, ADHD, Dyslexia, Giftedness, among others).

A vital developmental milestone. It is when a child and another person purposely focus their attention on the same object (e.g., the child points to an airplane in the sky and looks back at their mother to see if she is also looking). Deficits here are early warning signs for ASD.

The help an adult gives to ensure the child succeeds. It can be full physical prompt (holding their hand to do it together), visual prompt (pointing), vocal prompt (giving the first syllable), or gestural prompt. The goal is to prevent the child from failing and getting frustrated.

The art of gradually removing help so the child doesn't become dependent on the adult. For example, moving from holding their hand (physical prompt) to just pointing (visual prompt), until the child does it independently.

The child's ability to use a skill learned in the clinic in the real world. If they learn to use the clinic's toilet with the therapist but can't use it at school, they haven't generalized the skill yet.
The brain's ability to change, adapt, and create new connections. It is the reason why early intervention (starting therapies as early as possible) has such a massive impact on a child's future.
Actions that interrupt learning or routines, and that may put the child or others at risk (such as screaming very loudly, throwing objects, hitting others, or self-harming).

Stands for Antecedent (what happened right before), Behavior (what the child did), and Consequence (what happened right after). Used by therapists to figure out the reason behind a child's challenging behavior.
